a1_porch.title: The Last House on Marrow Street
a1_porch.text:
The door opens before your knuckles reach it, which is rude of it, or generous. Warm air comes out to meet you, smelling of cloves.

"Trick or treat," you say, as you have said at thirty doors tonight. Your friends wait under the lamp at the corner, pretending not to watch. At your feet grins a jack-o'-lantern with a flickering candle.

"Trick," says a polite voice from the dark inside. "Or treat." A pause. "Which would you prefer?"{{#if last_ending=become}} For half a breath it sounds like yours.{{else}}{{#if last_ending=consumed}} The house smells exactly as it did last time. Something has been kept warm for you.{{else}}{{#if last_ending=escape}} The door swings a little wider than it needs to, for someone who got away last time.{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}} A gloved hand comes to the edge of the light, palm up, patient as a collection plate.

choices.label: Trick
choices.beat: The gloved hand withdraws, empty.

a1_treat_hand.title: A Gloved Hand
a1_treat_hand.text:
The hand turns over and reveals three sweets wrapped in waxed paper twisted at both ends. They drop into your bag one at a time, each with the soft sound of a coin going into velvet. "Lovely," says the voice, and somewhere deep in the house a pen scratches one short line.

Behind you, without a sound, the top step has become the bottom of a long hill.

The glove turns palm up again. "May I take your coat?"

choices.label: Hand him your coat
choices.beat: "Lovely," says your host. The coat goes over his arm, and then it is gone, carried off down the hall to the hooks.

choices.label: Keep your coat on
choices.beat: The glove lowers, not in the least offended.

choices.label: Hold out your bag again
choices.beat: A fourth sweet drops into your bag. "Lovely," the voice says again, and deeper in, the pen scratches a second line.

a1_trick_laugh.title: Delight
a1_trick_laugh.text:
For a moment there is no sound from inside. Then laughter: a boy's laugh coming out of a gentleman's throat, from someone who has not heard that answer in a very long time.

"Trick," says the voice, tasting it. "Oh, well done. Then you'd better come in and play it." It adds, as if marking a card, "One to our visitor, nothing to the house."

Of all the lights on this porch, the jack-o'-lantern's candle is the only one moving with the wind. It is a stub of plain wax in a tin dish, and its light just reaches the rail, where somebody has left out a bowl of sweets.

choices.label: Rob the porch bowl
choices.beat: Two sweets come up from the bottom of the bowl. "One," your host counts from the doorway. "Two."

choices.label: Take the pumpkin's candle
choices.beat: The candle lifts out as if it had been waiting to be asked. Behind you the jack-o'-lantern goes dark.

a1_trick_porch.title: Light Fingers
a1_trick_porch.text:
Your host watches from the doorway, a dark shape with gloved hands folded. "A point to our visitor," he says, with real pleasure.{{#if candle}} When you hold the flame toward him, the hall at his back draws in to meet the light, until it is no longer than a hall in a house this size should be.{{/if}}

Down at the gate the path is still there, and so, for now, is the street.

choices.label: Take the candle too
choices.beat: The candle lifts out as if it had been waiting to be asked. Behind you the jack-o'-lantern goes dark.

choices.label: Empty the bowl too
choices.beat: The bowl gives up its last two sweets, heavier than sweets ought to be. "Two more to our visitor," your host says, delighted, as they go into your pocket.

a1_trick_path.title: The Path Back
a1_trick_path.text:
You go down the steps with your back to the open door, and nothing stops you. Halfway to the gate you look back once. The porch light is still on, and the warm air is still pouring out into the cold, as if the house would sooner heat the whole street than shut its door on you. Nobody stands in the doorway. Nobody calls you back, or calls you anything at all.{{#if candle}} The candle in your hand leans toward the house, the way it leaned for the wind.{{/if}}

A fine rain begins. At the corner your friends are arguing about whose turn it is, and none of them has looked up yet.

choices.label: Go back up the steps
choices.beat: You climb the steps again. The door has waited for you, exactly as open as you left it.

a1_name.title: The Threshold
a1_name.text:
Your host waits just beyond the threshold, and he is smaller than his voice. His evening coat was cut for a grown man and its tails brush the floor. His white gloves are a size too large, and his moustache has been drawn on in burnt cork.

"Call me Mr. Marrow," he says, and bows. {{#if stance=treat}}"And whom do I have the pleasure of, my guest?"{{else}}"And whom shall I say is visiting?"{{/if}} Along the wall a row of coats stirs on its hooks and settles again, listening. Your name is in your mouth, where it always is. It has never before felt so much like something you could put down.

a1_foyer.title: The Foyer
a1_foyer.text:
{{#if name}}"{{name}}," your host says, once, quietly.{{else}}{{#if name_given}}You give him nothing, and he bows to it as if nothing were a perfectly good name.{{else}}He has nothing to call you, and lets that be.{{/if}}{{/if}}{{#if name_key=douglas}} Then he goes very still. "A very good name," he says at last. "I knew a boy who had it." Along the wall, every coat hook stops.{{else}}{{#if name_key=dina}} Upstairs, something small stops what it was doing. "We have one of those," your host says, pleased. "She prefers Dee. You may too, by the end."{{else}}{{#if name_key=raissa}} Down the hall the pen pauses over the book. "There is a Raissa in it already," your host says. "Nineteen thirty-one. She has waited a long time for company."{{else}}{{#if name_key=eric}} Far off, behind glass and leaves, somebody laughs. "We have one of those too," your host says, less pleased. "He will tell you he was expecting you."{{else}}{{#if name_key=victoria}} The hall warms by a degree as he says it. "That name is said with great affection here," he says. "The house will mind its manners tonight."{{else}}{{#if name_key=steven}} Something like recognition crosses the burnt-cork face. "The architect," he says, and does not explain. "I wondered when you would come to see how it turned out."{{else}}{{#if name_key}} "Oh," says your host. "You were expected." He does not say by whom.{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}}

The foyer is the loveliest room you have ever set foot in. A chandelier cascades like a fountain above a floor of polished black-and-white tiles, strangely warm beneath your feet. A staircase curls upward, disappearing into the dark. Somewhere a waltz plays three bars and pauses.

Every clock in the room says 11:59. The one over the arch has a pendulum, and it hangs dead straight.

Brass hooks along the near wall are tagged 1898, 1931, 1953, 1979, each holding a coat left by someone who meant to come back. Opposite, three portraits have had their eyes painted out.

Your host stops under the arch and stands aside. "After you." Then, lightly: "Did anyone see you come up the path?"

choices.label: Say your friends saw you
choices.beat: "Your friends," your host repeats, and glances past you at the door as though they might be standing in it. "Then you have told me no lies."

choices.label: "Nobody saw me."
choices.beat: "Ah," says your host, and somewhere deeper in the house a pen is taken up.

choices.label: Say nothing
choices.beat: In the quiet, something under the floor knocks once and stops, as if remembering its manners. "Then you have told me no lies," says your host.

a1_push.title: First Through the Door
a1_push.text:
You shoulder past him before he can ask you anything. He flattens himself against the frame so that you never quite touch, and follows you in, laughing. "You went first," he says. "A point to our visitor."

The foyer is still catching up with you: the chandelier sways on its chain, the coats swing on their hooks, and somewhere further in a waltz starts a bar late. Only the clocks keep still. Every face says one minute to midnight, and the pendulum over the inner arch hangs dead straight while everything around it swings. On the far wall three portraits have had their eyes painted out.

"Did anyone see you come up the path?" he asks.

choices.label: Say your friends saw you
choices.beat: "Your friends," your host repeats, and glances past you at the door as though they might be standing in it. "Then you have told me no lies."

choices.label: "Nobody saw me."
choices.beat: "Ah," says your host, and somewhere deeper in the house a pen is taken up.

choices.label: Say nothing
choices.beat: In the quiet, something under the floor knocks once and stops, as if remembering its manners. "Then you have told me no lies," says your host.

a1_riddle.title: A Small Game

end_no_one_home.title: No One Home
end_no_one_home.text:
You do not look round. You keep your eyes on your friends under the lamp, who want to know what took you so long, and you find you have nothing to tell them.{{#if candy>=1}} The stolen sweets sit in a drawer for years, never eaten and never quite thrown away.{{/if}}{{#if candle}} The candle burns down that night on your windowsill, leaning with the wind.{{/if}}

You grow up and have a front door of your own, with a good lock. Every Halloween, at one minute to midnight, it swings open by itself and lets the warm out into the dark, politely, as if someone had knocked. Every year you get up and shut it. Every year it asks again.

ending.title: No One Home
ending.epitaph: Declined, with thanks. The door still asks.

a2_hub.title: Three Doors

choices.label: Follow the smell to the kitchen

a2_hub_2.title: Two Doors
a2_hub_2.text:
The parlor doors close behind you without a sound.{{#if clock}} Every clock in the foyer still says one minute to midnight, but one of them has begun to hum, the way a person taps a foot under a table.{{/if}}

Beside the stair, where there was only wall when you came in, an arch of ivy now stands open. Green light comes through it, the colour light turns after it has passed through a great many leaves, and now and then it shifts, as if the leaves were moving. Your host follows your eyes to it, then glances down the passage the bread smell comes from. "One or the other, I'm afraid," he says.

choices.label: Follow the smell to the kitchen

a2_hub_stair.title: The Stair
a2_hub_stair.text:
You come back into the foyer and notice there is one door fewer than there was. {{#unless ledger}}There is no firelight to the left any more.{{else}}{{#if wishbone}}The green light has gone from beside the stair.{{else}}The bread smell has gone out of the air.{{/if}}{{/unless}} Where that room's door stood there is wallpaper, matched to the rest so well you could not find the join.{{#if candle}} By your candle, the door shows through the paper anyway, faint as a watermark.{{/if}}

The velvet rope is down, and the stair climbs into the dark. {{#if stance=treat}}Your host offers you his arm. "It is dark on the stair, my guest," he says, like a man hoping to be refused.{{else}}Your host crooks his arm at you with a little bow, a move in the game. "Our visitor may take it, of course, though I think that would be a point to the house."{{/if}}

a2_parlor_book.title: The Guestbook
a2_parlor_book.text:
Your host opens the parlor doors and stands aside. "After you." Beside the fire a great book lies open, the way books lie open in churches.

It is a guestbook, and its first line, where a host would sign before any guest, is blank. Under it is one line in a boy's careful capitals, leaning right, dated 1898, and below it the names run down the years, each a little larger and less steady than the last, as though the signers needed more of the page to be sure they were there. Raissa Carvalho signed in 1931, in a round kitchen hand.{{#if name_given}} The next empty line is exactly the length of your name.{{/if}}{{#if stance=treat}} "The pen is just there, my guest."{{/if}}

choices.label: Sign your name
choices.beat: You sign below the newest name, a little larger than you meant to. "Lovely," says your host.

a2_parlor_pages.title: The First Page
a2_parlor_pages.text:
You turn back, leaf by leaf, to the first page and the boy's line under the blank one. One word of it can still be read: DOUGLAS. The rest is gone under a thumbprint, pressed into the ink while it was wet, and the print has the fine cross-weave of a cotton glove.

Behind you your host has stopped talking. When you look round he is watching the fire with his gloved hands folded, and one end of his burnt-cork moustache has smudged, as though he had touched it without meaning to. He does not ask you to sign. He does not ask you not to.

choices.label: Close the book
choices.beat: The book shuts with a soft clap of old paper, and a little dust goes up into the firelight.

choices.label: Sign your name under it
choices.beat: You sign below the newest name, a little larger than you meant to. "Lovely," says your host, to the fire.

a2_parlor_fire.title: The Stopped Clock
a2_parlor_fire.text:
In the corner stands a clock taller than your host, its face painted with a moon that has not risen in a long while. Its hands say one minute to midnight, and its pendulum hangs behind the glass as still as a held breath. Low on the dial is a keyhole with no key in it.

The key is on your host's watch chain, a small brass thing among the fobs. He sees you see it, and his glove goes to the chain and rests there. {{#if stance=treat}}"Anything you need, my guest?" he asks, hoping, for once, that there is not.{{else}}He smiles like a man across a chessboard with one finger on a piece.{{/if}}

choices.label: Ask for the clock key
choices.beat: With a small sigh he does not let himself finish, he unhooks the key and closes your fingers over it with both gloves. "Lovely."

choices.label: Lift the key from his chain
choices.beat: The chain swings out on his next gesture, and the key comes away in your fingers. He watches it go, and lets it.

choices.label: Leave the clock be
choices.beat: You leave the key on its chain, and the clock goes on saying one minute to midnight.

a2_parlor_false.title: A False Name
a2_parlor_false.text:
You write a name that is not yours, and the ink takes it without complaint. Your host reads it upside down. {{#if lies=1}}"Ah," he says, gently, as if a guest had dropped a spoon.{{#if debt>=1}} Then he takes the pen out of your fingers and puts it in his pocket. "So we are playing after all, and you are our visitor. Our visitor won't need this."{{/if}}{{else}}This time he does not say "Ah." He draws two short strokes in the margin, one for this name and one for the path.{{/if}}

He steps aside so that you can see the corner. A tall clock stands there saying one minute to midnight, its pendulum dead still behind the glass and a keyhole low on its dial. The key that fits it hangs on his watch chain, and he lets the chain swing where you can see it.

choices.label: Lift the key from his chain
choices.beat: The chain swings out on his next gesture, and the key comes away in your fingers. He watches it go, and lets it.

choices.label: Leave the clock be
choices.beat: You leave the key on its chain, and the clock goes on saying one minute to midnight.

a2_parlor_clock.title: The Key
a2_parlor_clock.text:
The key is warm from his waistcoat and heavier than it looks, plain brass, its bow worn smooth by somebody's thumb. You fit it to the keyhole without turning it, only to feel whether it goes home, and it goes home. Behind the glass the pendulum hangs and waits.

It is one minute to midnight and has been for a very long time, and in your hand is the thing that would let it be midnight. Your host says nothing at all, which is the loudest thing he has done tonight.{{#if lied}} He is watching the clock, not you, as if it might be about to say something about you.{{/if}}

choices.label: Wind the clock
choices.beat: The key turns stiffly, then easily. Deep in the case something winds tight with a long ratcheting purr, and the clock ticks once, and holds. Your host flinches.

choices.label: Put the key back
choices.beat: You hang the key back on his chain yourself, and he lets you.

a2_parlor_leave.title: Settling Up
a2_parlor_leave.text:
Your host turns the guestbook to a narrow column beside the signatures that you had taken for a margin. It is headed in faded copperplate: Received.

{{#if debt>=1}}Under it, in his careful capitals, runs a short column of entries that are yours, beginning with the sweets at the door. The newest is so fresh the ink still shines. "Sweets settle it," he says. "One sweet strikes out one line, here or at the table downstairs. Nothing else will do, I'm afraid." He uncaps the pen and holds it over the oldest entry, and he looks sorry, the way a host is sorry to see a guest reach for a coat.{{else}}Under it there is nothing of yours at all. "Our visitor owes the house nothing," he says, and the pen stays capped. Behind him the fire goes on burning for nobody.{{/if}} Over the mantel the painted family waits for you to go.

choices.label: Pay one sweet
choices.beat: You lay a sweet on the page, and he draws one neat line through the oldest entry. He does not say "Lovely." It is not a word for being paid.

choices.label: Pay two sweets
choices.beat: You lay two sweets on the page, and he strikes two lines through, slowly. He does not say "Lovely." It is not a word for being paid.

choices.label: Warm your hands at his fire
choices.beat: You hold your hands to his fire without asking. It warms them thoroughly, finger by finger, the way a thing is done when someone is keeping count.

choices.label: Bid the portraits goodnight
choices.beat: Nobody answers. At the door you look back, and every portrait hangs a little crooked on its nail, turned to watch you go.

a2_kitchen_door.title: The Cook
a2_kitchen_door.text:
The passage ends in the warmest room yet, where a black range glows and a table is laid for one. A woman in a tea-towel turban stands at the dresser wiping her hands on her apron. Her hands are perfectly clean, and she goes on wiping them, slowly, the way you would rub at a mark only you can see. She hums three bars of the waltz, stops, and counts the spoons.

{{#if stance=treat}}"Sit yourself down, duck," she says, and pulls out the one chair. "You can call me the cook."{{else}}"I don't serve strangers," she tells the wall, and keeps her back to you. Behind her the range is crowded, and nobody is watching it.{{/if}} {{#if ledger}}You saw her name in the guestbook, and would guess that nobody has said it to her in a very long time.{{else}}She tugs the tea towel straighter on her head. "I came as a fortune-teller, you know. Yours is a short one."{{/if}}

choices.label: Sit down to eat
choices.beat: She sets a plate in front of you and stands back to watch you eat. Down the passage, faintly, someone says "Lovely."

choices.label: Raid the stove
choices.beat: Two sweets come off the warming shelf, still warm in their twisted paper. At the dresser the counting goes on.

a2_kitchen_thanks.title: Raissa

choices.label: Stay and eat with her
choices.beat: She fills a plate before you can change your mind. Down the passage, faintly, someone says "Lovely."

choices.label: Taste from the pot
choices.beat: You take one spoonful straight from the open pot, too hot to be sensible. At the dresser she goes very still, and does not turn round.

a2_kitchen_feast.title: Seconds
a2_kitchen_feast.text:
It is the best thing you have ever tasted: new bread, a clove or two, and something slow that has been on the stove since before you were born. Idly you try to picture your own front door, and find you cannot say what colour it is. You know there is a door. The colour has simply gone out of it, like a lamp in another room, and that does not seem to matter much.

{{#if stance=trick}}The cook has turned round to look at you.{{/if}} "I'll tell you plainly, because nobody told me," she says. "One plate and you'll forget your way home. Two, and you'll forget yourself entirely." She takes a clean tea towel from the end of the dresser and lays it folded beside your plate like an invitation.

choices.label: Push the plate away
choices.beat: You push the plate away. It takes more doing than it should, and the cook lets out a breath she has been holding.

a2_kitchen_bone.title: The Wishbone
a2_kitchen_bone.text:
{{#if stance=treat}}She takes your hand, turns it to the light of the range, and reads it the way you would read a recipe you know by heart.{{else}}She does not turn round, for a question or for a hand in her pans. She tells your fortune to the wall.{{/if}} "It's all about supper," she says. "Whoever eats here forgets the way home. That's the whole of it." She wipes her clean hands. "It's very good food." She says that part like an apology.

On a saucer by the range a wishbone is drying, small and clean, the forked kind you pull with someone to make a wish. {{#if stance=treat}}"Take it, duck. A present." Down the passage a pen lifts, and waits.{{else}}Her back stays turned, and behind her the pot simmers, smelling of every supper you ever came in to out of the dark.{{/if}}

choices.label: Accept the wishbone
choices.beat: It is light as paper in your palm. Down the passage, faintly, someone says "Lovely."

choices.label: Pocket the wishbone
choices.beat: The wishbone goes into your pocket while her back is turned. She counts one spoon twice, and does not turn round.

choices.label: Taste from the pot
choices.beat: You take one spoonful straight from the pot, too hot to be sensible. At the dresser the counting stops in the middle of a number.

choices.label: Leave it on the saucer
choices.beat: You leave the wishbone where it lies, and the cook nods once, to the saucer.

a2_kitchen_floor.title: Under the Flagstones
a2_kitchen_floor.text:
Three knocks come up through the flagstones, slow and polite, close enough that you feel them in your heels before you hear them. The cook goes white and grips a spoon.

"Don't you go answering that," she says. "Nothing in this house goes through a door it wasn't asked through, and every knock you give back is asking. Three, and it comes up to meet you. All my years here I've never answered, and nobody's ever asked it what it wants." The flagstone under your feet is warm as a loaf under a cloth.{{#if fed}} You find you would quite like to knock back. It seems only polite.{{/if}}

choices.label: Knock back
choices.beat: You knock once on the warm stone. The floor says "Welcome" in the cook's voice, though her mouth is shut. She walks you back to the foyer without a word.

choices.label: Knock back
choices.beat: You kneel and knock once on the warm stone. Cloves and new bread rise between the flags, and the floor says "Welcome" in the cook's voice. Her mouth is shut.

choices.label: Leave it unanswered
choices.beat: You step off the warm stone. The cook lets out her breath and walks you back up the passage to the foyer.

choices.label: Leave it unanswered
choices.beat: You step off the warm stone. The cook lets out her breath, and after a long moment the floor settles.

a2_cons_door.title: Eric
a2_cons_door.text:
You go in under the arch of ivy beside the stair, and the room beyond it is made of glass. Vines grow flat against the panes, and they lean toward your warmth, the way sunflowers turn. Far back among them sits a boy in a skeleton suit whose painted bones stopped glowing years ago, a candle in a tin dish on his knee. "Eric," he says, and taps the dish twice. "Only light in the place that doesn't belong to the house. Keeps it out of here, mostly."

{{#if stance=treat}}{{#if fed}}He sniffs the air, and his face falls. "Aw, man. You ate." He holds the dish out anyway. "Promise you won't again. Somebody's got to carry it."{{else}}His grin goes a little sorry. "Guest, huh. Oh, man. This candle's yours if you promise never to eat in this house. A promise to me doesn't count as a debt."{{/if}}{{else}}He grins. "Another stranger. Outstanding." He holds the dish out to you.{{#if candle}} Your flame and his lean toward each other across the gap, like two people about to whisper.{{/if}}{{/if}}

choices.label: Promise never to eat here
choices.beat: You promise: no more eating in this house. Eric taps the dish twice, puts it in your hands, and disappears into the vines, looking relieved.

choices.label: Take the candle
choices.beat: The dish is warm and lighter than it looks. Eric sits back with his hands empty, says "Outstanding," and disappears into the vines, still grinning.

choices.label: Ask how he fools the house
Leave him his light
choices.beat: "Suit yourself, man," says Eric, and cups his hand round the flame again.

a2_cons_lesson.title: The Lie Trick

choices.label: Promise for the candle
choices.beat: You promise: no more eating in this house. Eric taps the dish twice, puts it in your hands, and disappears into the vines, looking relieved.

choices.label: Take the candle
choices.beat: The dish is warm and lighter than it looks. Eric sits back with his hands empty, says "Outstanding," and disappears into the vines, still grinning.

choices.label: Let him keep it
choices.beat: "Suit yourself, man," says Eric, and cups his hand round the flame again.

a2_cons_out.title: Find Anything
a2_cons_out.text:
Your host is waiting just outside the glass, the toes of his evening shoes lined up along the brass sill and not a hair over. The vines nearest the door have drawn back from him, the way a cat draws back from a hand it does not know.{{#if candle}} He does not look at the candle, very carefully.{{/if}}{{#if lied}} His pen is uncapped before you have said a word.{{/if}}

"I don't go in there," he says, as if you had asked. "I've never been asked." Then, lightly: "Find anything?" He asked about the path just as lightly, and he waits now in the same way, ready to write down whatever you tell him.

choices.label: Say nothing
choices.beat: You say nothing at all. Your host holds his pen over the page a moment longer, then caps it and stands aside for you. "After you."

a2_cons_lie.title: Only Vines
a2_cons_lie.text:
Your host writes it down in careful capitals: ONLY VINES. {{#if lies=1}}"Ah," he says.{{#if debt>=1}} "Then we are playing after all, and you are our visitor." The arm he had half offered you, a guest's arm, goes back to his side.{{/if}}{{else}}This time he does not say "Ah." He underlines it, once for each story you have told him tonight, and looks rather pleased with you.{{/if}}

He walks you back to a foyer with one door fewer. {{#if ledger}}The bread smell has gone out of the air, and the passage it came down is papered over, the paste still wet.{{else}}The firelight has gone from the left, and where the parlor doors stood there is wallpaper, the paste still wet.{{/if}} The velvet rope is down. At the foot of the stair he crooks his elbow at you with a little bow.

end_seconds.title: Seconds
end_seconds.text:
You were told plainly, and you hold out your plate anyway.{{#if stance=trick}} She takes it and looks you properly in the face.{{/if}} Then, slowly, the cook smiles. It is the first smile since 1931, and it takes years off her, and then it takes all of them.

She fills the plate. Then she unties her apron and ties it on you, the way you would for a child helping with the baking, and puts the clean tea towel in your hands. She sits down in the chair by the range and closes her eyes. The spoons want counting. Out in the foyer the front door is opening for someone new, and you already know what they will want for supper.

ending.title: Seconds
ending.epitaph: There was always room for more.

a3_hall.title: The Upstairs Hall
a3_hall.text:
{{#if candle}}The candle does not make the hall any brighter. It makes it shorter. By this small honest flame the hall is no longer than the house is wide, and it ends at a window with rain on it.{{else}}The runner under your feet is softer than carpet ought to be. The stair is still gone behind you, and you find that you do not mind; you cannot quite remember what you wanted it for.{{/if}} Halfway along, cold comes under a door, the flat, still cold of a great deal of glass.

{{#if name_given}}The door nearest the landing is narrower than the others and painted white. Across the middle, in a child's careful capitals, with a pencil line ruled underneath to keep them straight, someone has lettered a name. {{#if name}}It is {{name}}.{{else}}It says OUR GUEST, in case a better one turns up.{{/if}}{{else}}The door nearest the landing has no handle. Someone has papered over the place where one would go, matching the roses so carefully that they run on unbroken. Somewhere overhead, a girl is humming three bars of a waltz, and stopping, and starting again.{{/if}}

a3_hall_long.title: The Long Hall
a3_hall_long.text:
The hall runs away from the landing over a red runner worn pale down the middle. You count the doors to have something to count, and at twelve you stop, because you have seen this house from the street and it is not as wide as this. Halfway along, a portrait of a man in an evening coat looks down at you with his eyes painted out. When you look back, the stair has gone, and there is only more hall.

Your host is nowhere in it, though he would come if you called. He is that kind of host.{{#if name_given}} Somewhere ahead, the house is practising your name under its breath, getting the vowels right.{{/if}}

choices.label: Eat a sweet to steady yourself
choices.beat: The sweet tastes of cloves. While you chew, the hall draws in door by door, until it is exactly as long as the house is wide.

choices.label: Call for your host
choices.beat: You say it once, not loudly, and he is at your elbow before the word has finished, offering his arm.

choices.label: Call for your host
choices.beat: You say it once, not loudly, and he is at your elbow before the word has finished, offering his arm.

a3_hall_dark.title: The Same Hall
a3_hall_dark.text:
It is the same hall, and you know it by the portrait. The man in the evening coat hangs where he hung, his eyes still painted out, but the coat he wears is not an evening coat any more. It is the twin of yours, down to the pulled thread at the cuff.

{{#if name_given}}Behind you, quite close, someone says your name the way you would say it across a room to someone you were fond of, and you turn before you have decided to. {{/if}}{{#if stance=treat}}Hands you cannot see take you by the shoulders, gently, as a host steers a guest out of the wrong room, and set you down in front of two doors.{{else}}Nothing steers you. Two doors stand at your elbow, and past the last candle the dark holds a door of its own open.{{#if fear>=8}} It looks restful, and nobody has put anything in its way.{{/if}}{{/if}}

a3_hall_arm.title: His Arm
a3_hall_arm.text:
Through the sleeve, your host's arm is thinner than it looks. It is a boy's wrist in a man's cuff, and the cuff has been turned back four times to make it fit. {{#if stance=treat}}"Mind the runner, my guest," he says, though there is nothing wrong with the runner.{{else}}"And that is a point to the house," he tells the portraits as you pass, pleased with himself.{{/if}}{{#if candle}} All the way along he keeps his face turned from your flame.{{/if}}

He walks you until the hall is no longer than the house is wide, then stops at the nearest door and steps back from it. "After you." {{#if name_given}}Your name is painted on it in a child's careful capitals, with a pencil line ruled underneath to keep them straight.{{else}}It has no handle, only a smooth place where a handle would go, and he regards it with polite regret.{{/if}}

a3_hall_2.title: Two Doors Left
a3_hall_2.text:
The nursery door shuts behind you with a small, decided click.{{#if trust<=-2}} Then a key turns in it, on the inside.{{/if}}

The hall is shorter than it was. Cold comes under the mirror room's door, and at the far end the attic steps stand open now, going up into the sound of rain. Behind you, at the landing end, too far off for any light to reach, the house has begun to take the hall away. The runner is lifting from the boards and rolling itself up, the way a runner is rolled up after a party. By the look of the runner, you have time for only one more room.

a3_nursery_door.title: The Nursery
a3_nursery_door.text:
The paint in here is new enough to smell, and the moon in the window is a little too round, the moon as you would draw it. The room was made for you the moment you gave your name. Somebody is in the crib already.

She is a girl in a bedsheet ghost, and the eyeholes are cut crooked, one higher than the other, as if she had done them herself. {{#if stance=treat}}"You're a guest too," she whispers. "Don't take anything else off him. He's nice. That's how he does it."{{else}}She bends to peer at you through the lower eyehole. "You're not a guest," she says, delighted. "I can tell. Good. Somebody ought to trick him for once."{{/if}}{{#if candle}} By your candle there is nothing behind the eyeholes at all, and the sheet sits up anyway.{{/if}}

choices.label: Say hello
choices.beat: You say hello as quietly as she whispered, and she whispers it back.

choices.label: Say boo
choices.beat: You say boo, and she laughs into the sheet, the muffled laugh of an accomplice.

choices.label: Give her a sweet
choices.beat: She tucks the sweet away under the sheet, quickly, before anyone can count it.

choices.label: Laugh at the sheet
choices.beat: You laugh, and the eyeholes droop, the way a sad face does. Nobody else ever comes up here, though, so after a while she talks to you anyway.

a3_nursery_pip.title: Is It Still Halloween

choices.label: "It's still 1953."
choices.beat: She lets out a breath she must have been holding a long time, and the sheet sags with it. "Oh, good," she says. "I thought it was ever so late."

choices.label: Say it's still Halloween
choices.beat: It is still Halloween, strictly speaking. She knows that it is not the whole truth, and decides not to ask for the rest.

choices.label: Knock back on the wall
choices.beat: You knock three times on the wallpaper, the way it knocked. The wall answers once, softer, and the smell of warm bread comes through the paper.

a3_nursery_year.title: Seventy-Three

choices.label: Take her ribbon
choices.beat: You promise properly. She puts the ribbon into your hand and folds your fingers over it, the way you would hand over something that might blow away.

choices.label: Leave her at the window
choices.beat: She does not turn round when you go, and she does not say goodbye.

a3_nursery_window.title: Her Porch Light
a3_nursery_window.text:
Dee goes to the window and kneels on the chair there, with her eyeholes to the glass. "There," she says. "Past the lamp." {{#if fed}}Where she looks you see only a soft grey nothing, with nothing written on it yet. Her face, through the sheet, is turned toward it and shining.{{else}}The street below runs on further than any street should, down a long hill of roofs, and right at the end of it, so small it could be a star come down too low, is a porch light in a little iron cage, still on.{{/if}}

"She always leaves it on till the last one's in." {{#if trust<=-2}}Then she turns from you to the wall and says, quite clearly, "They're in here." Somewhere in the house a pen moves.{{else}}{{#if trust=1}}She winds a ribbon round her fingers, as if she might give it to you, and does not hold it out, not yet.{{else}}She keeps her hands flat on the glass and does not look round.{{/if}}{{/if}}

choices.label: Leave her at the window
choices.beat: She does not turn round when you go, and she does not say goodbye.

a3_nursery_stay.title: A While
a3_nursery_stay.text:
You sit down on the floor by her chair. Neither of you says anything for a long while, long enough for one of your feet to go to sleep, and above the crib the little clock says one minute to midnight the whole time. When at last you look up at it again, its hands have not moved at all. {{#if fed}}She watches the grey nothing beyond the glass, and you watch her.{{else}}Far down the street, the caged porch light is still on.{{/if}}

{{#if trust>=2}}In the end she lays her ribbon across one palm and rests that hand on the floor between you, where you could reach it. "Only if you mean it," she says.{{else}}{{#if trust>=0}}After a while the sheet leans against your shoulder, a little. The ribbon stays wound round her fingers.{{else}}She lets you sit, and does not say anything to you at all.{{/if}}{{/if}}

choices.label: Take her ribbon
choices.beat: You promise properly. She puts the ribbon into your hand and folds your fingers over it, the way you would hand over something that might blow away.

choices.label: Say goodnight
choices.beat: "Goodnight," she says back, as if you will both see each other in the morning.

choices.label: Slip out while she watches
choices.beat: She is still watching the window when you reach the door. She pretends she does not see you go.

a3_mirror_door.title: The Other Guest
a3_mirror_door.text:
Every wall in here is mirror, and the back of the door as well, so the room's few candles burn by the hundred. Old glass always shivers a little when someone walks past it, but this glass holds as still as water nobody has touched. {{#if fed}}Where you should be, it shows a front door with a brass number and a worn step. You know this door is yours, though until a minute ago you had forgotten it.{{else}}You lift your hand, and your reflection lifts its hand half a second after you, as if it had to look first. You lift it again, and this time its hand is already up.{{/if}}

{{#if stance=treat}}"I'd only like a word," it says, in your voice. "You'd be doing me a kindness."{{else}}"Go on, then," it says, in your voice. "You first. Or me. Let's see who's quicker."{{/if}}{{#if riddle=right}} It lets that sit a moment. "I knew it was the clock, downstairs, same as you," it adds. "We think alike."{{else}} It lets that sit a moment. "I guessed the same as you, downstairs," it adds. "We think alike."{{/if}}

choices.label: Make it go first
choices.beat: You keep perfectly still and wait for it to move. It waits too, for longer than you would have thought anyone could, and then it gives in and speaks first.

choices.label: Look for your front door
choices.beat: You find the door in the glass and hold on to it: the brass number, the worn step, a light above it, still on.

a3_mirror_offer.title: The Trade
a3_mirror_offer.text:
{{#if fed}}The front door in the glass stays where it is the whole time, and only the voice is yours.{{else}}Your reflection lays its palm flat against the inside of the glass, and the glass does not shiver.{{/if}}

"Here's the offer," it says, plainly, without any of the house's manners. "Let me keep your reflection. The house doesn't like letting people leave. But it counts heads, not faces, so it will count one of us as staying, and you will be able to leave this place. The price is your face. You'll never see it again, not in glass or water or a dark window, not even in a spoon. You'll have to take other people's word for what you look like."{{#if ribbon}} It has seen the ribbon. "Or one of us could stay in her place. Think about that."{{/if}}

choices.label: Let it keep your reflection
choices.beat: You nod, and that is all it takes. "Thank you," it says, in your voice, and after that the glass has nobody in it at all.

choices.label: Let it keep your reflection
choices.beat: You nod, and that is all it takes. "Thank you," it says, in your voice, and after that the glass has nobody in it at all.

a3_mirror_back.title: Your Back
a3_mirror_back.text:
Turning your back on a room made of mirror does not help. {{#if fed}}No wall shows any of you. In the glass of the door your own front door waits, and the voice comes out of it.{{else}}Every wall shows you the back of your own head, the collar and the parting in your hair, all of it half a second late. Only the glass in the door shows your face, and your face is watching you.{{/if}}

"Suit yourself," it says to the back of your head. "I'll be quick, then. The house counts heads, not faces. Let me keep your reflection and it will count one of us as staying, and you can go. The price is your face, for good.{{#if ribbon}} Or one of us could stay in her place. Think about that.{{/if}} You'd have to turn round to say yes."

choices.label: Let it keep your reflection
choices.beat: You nod, and that is all it takes. "Thank you," it says, in your voice, and after that the glass has nobody in it at all.

choices.label: Let it keep your reflection
choices.beat: You nod, and that is all it takes. "Thank you," it says, in your voice, and after that the glass has nobody in it at all.

a3_mirror_no.title: No
a3_mirror_no.text:
{{#if stance=treat}}"Oh," it says, in your voice, and it sounds hurt. "You'd have been doing me a kindness. Only a small one."{{else}}"Your move, then," it says, in your voice, amused. "I'll wait. I'm good at waiting."{{/if}} {{#if fed}}The front door in the glass begins, very slightly, to fade, like a photograph left in a sunny window.{{else}}It stays half a second late a moment longer, to show you that it can, and then, pointedly, it keeps perfect time.{{/if}}{{#if ribbon}} "If you want her to leave, she'll need someone in her chair, you know," it adds.{{/if}}

It does not argue any further. None of the candles in the glass has moved since you came in, and they do not move now. "The offer stands," it says, quite patiently, "right up until you leave this room."

choices.label: Give it your reflection after all
choices.beat: You nod, and that is all it takes. "Thank you," it says, in your voice, and after that the glass has nobody in it at all.

choices.label: Give it your reflection after all
choices.beat: You nod, and that is all it takes. "Thank you," it says, in your voice, and after that the glass has nobody in it at all.

a3_attic_stair.title: The Trunks

choices.label: Read the tag by candlelight
choices.beat: The roof goes white, and by your own small flame you read it: DOUGLAS A. TULL, AGE 11, printed the way a boy prints when he has been told to.

choices.label: Match the hand to the guestbook
choices.beat: With the guestbook's 1898 line in mind, the leaning capitals give themselves up: DOUGLAS A. TULL, AGE 11, printed the way a boy prints when told to.

choices.label: Tell the boards the year
choices.beat: Under the boards the girl goes quiet for a long time after you tell her. Then, very small: "That's not an hour."

a3_attic_floor.title: Rain on the Roof

choices.label: Knock back on the floor
choices.beat: You knock once on the warm boards, slow and polite, the way it knocked. Far below, something that has waited a long while settles, pleased.

a3_hatch.title: The Hatch
a3_hatch.text:
When you come out, the hall has gone. Where it was, there is a square hatch in the floorboards with a brass ring set flush in one corner, and warm air comes up round its edges like breath: in, and a long pause, and out. On the out-breath you smell bread and cloves. Whatever door you did not open tonight has been papered over, and the pattern is not quite matched at the seams.

{{#if mirror}}The polished brass ring shows the ceiling, and the papered walls, and nobody bending over it. {{/if}}{{#if trust>=1}}A small figure in a bedsheet ghost crouches by the hatch, though you did not hear her come. She looks at you through the crooked eyeholes, and points down.{{else}}{{#if trust<=-2}}The hatch already stands open a hand's width. Someone has told those below that you are coming.{{/if}}{{/if}}

end_lights_out.title: Lights Out
end_lights_out.text:
You walk on past the last candle, and nobody stops you, because nobody has to. The runner ends, and then the boards, and then there is only the sound of your feet on something that answers like boards. You put a hand out to the wall. It is there, and then it is a little further away than it was, and then it is not there.

You stop counting doors, and then steps, and somewhere you could not have named you stop being the one who counts. Far back, in a gilt frame, a portrait has a new sitter in your coat, with the eyes painted out.

ending.title: Lights Out
ending.epitaph: Walked the hall. The hall walked further.

a4_cellar.title: The Cellar

a4_jars.title: The Jars
a4_jars.text:
Each label is tied on with string and gives a date and a street in careful capitals. *OCT. 31, 1931. ORCHARD LANE.* Inside that jar something very small goes round and round the glass, and when you lean close you know it for a sound: a woman calling a name across a garden at dusk.

One jar, dated 1953, is full of sweets in waxed paper, twisted at both ends and never spent.{{#if trust>=1}} The sheet at your elbow goes very still. "Those are mine," Dee whispers. "For when I get home."{{/if}}{{#if fed}} At the end of the shelf stands a new jar, its lid still bright. The label is a street you do not recognise, and you are sure you should.{{/if}}

choices.label: Hold your own jar
choices.beat: You lift the bright jar, and for as long as you hold it you can name the street. When you set it down, the name stays in the glass.

a4_jars_sweets.title: Nineteen Fifty-Three

choices.label: Give them to her
choices.beat: Dee takes the sweets under the sheet without a word. Then, very quietly, she says thank you, the way somebody taught her to.

choices.label: Put them back
choices.beat: You drop the sweets back into the jar and screw the lid down tight. On the shelf it stops turning.

a4_door.title: The Green Door
a4_door.text:
The roots end at a door painted the dark green of a front door on a good street, with a brass plate, a handle, and no keyhole.{{#if candle}} By your candle the green is translucent, and through it you can see the end of a long table, laid.{{/if}}

From the other side comes a knock, then another, then a third. After that there is only the quiet of someone waiting on a step with folded hands.{{#if knocks>=3}} Your hand goes flat on the warm paint. You have answered three times tonight, and these knocks came from higher up than the others, as if whatever makes them has already started to climb.{{else}}{{#if knocks>=2}} Your hand goes flat on the warm paint. You have answered twice tonight, and the door waits under your palm for the third.{{/if}}{{/if}}

choices.label: Knock back
choices.beat: You knock back once, as it did. The quiet on the other side changes, the way a room goes quiet when the guest it was waiting for walks in.

choices.label: Wait for it to open
choices.beat: You fold your hands, as the knocking did, and let it be somebody else's move. After a long moment the handle turns from within.

a4_table.title: The Long Table
a4_table.text:
The door swings inward, and a great kind heat comes out. Beyond it runs a table so long that its far end is only a rumour, laid for hundreds, with a card at every place. The nearest cards say *R. CARVALHO* and *MISS D. ASHDOWN* and *E. OKAFOR*. Halfway down, one chair has been pulled all the way out for you. {{#if name}}Its card says *{{name}}*, spelled right.{{else}}Its card is blank, and propped up with care.{{/if}}

From the head of the table Mr. Marrow bows you in. "After you." Beside your plate he has opened a book bound in green cloth, and a silver lid is keeping the plate warm. {{#if debt>=1}}Your page holds a short column of pen strokes in his careful hand.{{#if candle}} Eric's candle leans away from the lid.{{/if}}{{else}}Your page is blank, and he looks at it a long moment without saying "Lovely."{{/if}}

choices.label: Leave the book as it is
Taste what's on your plate
choices.beat: You lift the lid and eat, and whatever you still knew of the way home goes out like a lamp in another room. "Lovely," says Mr. Marrow.

choices.label: Taste what's on your plate
choices.beat: You lift the lid and eat, and whatever you still knew of the way home goes out like a lamp in another room. Nobody writes it down.

a4_table_book.title: The Green Book
a4_table_book.text:
Mr. Marrow turns the green book round to face you. Each stroke on your page is a kindness you said yes to, entered the moment you said it, and beside every one he has written the same small word in the margin: *Lovely.* He uncaps the pen. "You can pay in sweets to settle your debt," he says. "One sweet strikes out one line."

He is honest about the rest.{{#if stance=trick}} "A visitor's page, settled, is still a visitor's page. It will not make you a guest again."{{else}} "Settling keeps a guest's page clean. But whether you are let out is midnight's business."{{#unless clock}} He caps the pen a moment, and uncaps it again. "And midnight is not coming tonight."{{/unless}}{{/if}}

choices.label: Pay one sweet
choices.beat: He takes one sweet from your palm, as carefully as a coin from a child, and draws one neat line through.

choices.label: Pay two sweets
choices.beat: He takes two sweets from your palm, as carefully as coins from a child, and draws two neat lines through.

choices.label: Pay three sweets
choices.beat: He takes three sweets from your palm, as carefully as coins from a child, and draws three neat lines through.

choices.label: Keep your sweets
choices.beat: He caps the pen without a word, the way a shopkeeper does when you only came in to look.

a4_gate.title: The Final Gate

a4_gate_name.title: Douglas Ashby Tull

choices.label: Say nothing
choices.beat: You say nothing. He waits for an order that does not come, and then, carefully, he puts Mr. Marrow back on like a coat.

a4_gate_light.title: The Honest Flame
a4_gate_light.text:
You hold up the candle, and the Marrow shrinks to its real size. The table is a plank on trestles with twenty places, and the hundreds were those twenty over and over, the way a room repeats between two mirrors. At the far end, painted to look like brick, is a door.{{#if ribbon}} By the flame you see Dee beside you, her sheet empty under the light, the ribbon still held.{{/if}}{{#if mirror}} Near the foot of the table someone with your face is already seated.{{/if}}

Mr. Marrow shades his eyes. "Not one of ours, that," he says, and does not ask you to put it out.{{#if stance=treat}} "A guest leaves by the front door, at the proper hour. The flame is for strangers."{{/if}}

choices.label: Blow it out
choices.beat: You blow the candle out. The Marrow comes back all at once, long and laid and glowing, as if it had only stepped out of the room.

a4_gate_midnight.title: Midnight
a4_gate_midnight.text:
The clock behind Mr. Marrow lets go of its minute hand. It strikes, and every clock in the house answers at once, after a hundred and twenty-eight years of standing still. The candles bow. Mr. Marrow holds your chair like the rail of a ship.

"Midnight," he says between strokes. "It lets go of every guest who owes nothing, and anyone holding a living promise to leave. It forgives nothing else."{{#if stance=trick}} "Guests, mind you, and you are only our visitor. It is particular."{{/if}}{{#if lied}} After each stroke the clock pauses, as if it were reading back the lie in his book.{{/if}}{{#if debt>=1}} Beside your plate the green book falls open again, at your page.{{/if}} At the far end of the room a door stands open on the cold. "Only once," he says.

choices.label: Let it strike
choices.beat: You let it strike. On the twelfth stroke the door at the far end of the room swings shut, and then it is only wall.

a4_gate_seat.title: Your Seat
a4_gate_seat.text: You sit, and the chair takes you all at once, the way a warm bath does. Mr. Marrow pushes it in until your knees are under the cloth and lays the napkin in your lap, and then he stands back to see what you have brought to the table. {{#if fed}}Your plate smells exactly like everything you have already eaten tonight, and like more of it, and your hand is already near the fork.{{else}}You have not touched a crumb all night, and your plate has gone on steaming anyway, patiently, as if it knew you would come round.{{/if}}{{#if knocks>=3}} Under your feet, under the cloth, there is a hatch in the floor, and something on the other side of it is waiting very politely to be let up.{{/if}} Behind you the cellar is dark and long, and nobody is guarding it.

end_housewarming.title: Housewarming
end_housewarming.text:
"Fetch the guestbook," you tell him, by his name, and Douglas fetches it, held to his chest like a hymnal. You knock once on the table, the fourth knock, the first ever started from this side. You snap the wishbone, wish the house a name of its own, and write it on the first line. *Marrow.*

The warmth goes out of the room like a sigh. Raissa unties her apron. Among vines you never saw, a candle goes out, and a sheet with crooked eyeholes runs for the stair. Douglas is eleven for one second, and then he is dust in a good coat. Nobody says "Lovely." You walk out into an ordinary morning, and only you remember their names.

ending.title: Housewarming
ending.epitaph: Here stood a welcome. It finally went home.

end_all_hallows.title: All Hallows
end_all_hallows.text:
The clock strikes, and your reflection gets up from its chair. It comes down the table with your walk and sits in Dee's chair. The house counts, and the count is right.

You go out together through a door that is there only for the length of a bell, and the street outside is two streets at once: wet leaves and a car alarm, and 1953, a privet hedge and a house with its porch light on. Her mother left it on. Dee lets go of the ribbon and runs up the path, and the door opens before she reaches it. Just as it shuts, the light goes out.

You never see your own face again, in any glass.

ending.title: All Hallows
ending.epitaph: She left the light on. You never saw yourself again.

end_settled_account.title: Settled Account
end_settled_account.text:
Midnight finds you at the table with nothing written against you, and so the house has to bow. Mr. Marrow draws himself up to the whole of his eleven years and bows from the waist. "Thank you for coming," he says. He does not say "Lovely." There is nothing to write down.{{#if ribbon}} At the threshold the ribbon in your hand goes slack.{{/if}}{{#if mirror}} In the dark glass of the front door, nobody walks out beside you.{{/if}}

You go down the path alone, past a jack-o'-lantern gone dark, and the air smells only of leaves.{{#if name_given}} Every year after, a cream envelope comes in a careful schoolboy hand. *Do call again. —M.* You keep every one.{{/if}}

ending.title: Settled Account
ending.epitaph: Paid up, and politely shown out.

end_long_way_round.title: The Long Way Round
end_long_way_round.text:
The door opens exactly as far as it must, and no further. You go up through rooms that stand back to let you pass: the cellar, the stair, a hall only four doors long, the front step.{{#if ribbon}} At the top of the cellar stair the ribbon in your hand pulls once, back toward the table, and goes slack.{{/if}} You ate nothing in the house, so you still know the way.

You walk home in the rain, and the porch light is on. People are kind to you. They lend you umbrellas and hold doors, and not one of them, ever, asks you to stay for dinner.{{#if true_name}} Every Halloween, at one minute to midnight, you say his name once, to nobody.{{/if}}

ending.title: The Long Way Round
ending.epitaph: Never fed. Never kept. Never asked in.

end_head_count.title: Head Count
end_head_count.text:
Your reflection draws its chair in to the long table and smooths the cloth with your hands. It does not look at you.

You hold up the candle and walk. By its light the stair is short and the hall upstairs is only four doors long. A guest came down to the table and a guest is sitting at it, and the house, counting, does not look up.{{#if ribbon}} Halfway up the cellar stair the ribbon in your hand goes slack, trailing back into the dark toward a chair with a cushion on it.{{else}} You do not look back, and the house does not ask you to.{{/if}} On the front step the candle goes out. Afterwards nothing shows you: not windows, not puddles, not the back of a spoon.

ending.title: Head Count
ending.epitaph: One went home. One stayed. Neither was all of you.

end_new_host.title: The New Host
end_new_host.text:
"Go," you tell him, by his name. "Get out."

Douglas looks at you a moment. Then he takes off his gloves one finger at a time and lays them on the cloth, and shrugs out of his father's coat, and he is a thin boy in shirtsleeves with burnt cork on his lip. He goes first through a doorway, for the first time in a hundred and twenty-eight years.

You turn to follow him, and there is no way out that you can remember. Far above, someone knocks at the front door. The coat is nearly your size. Someone hands you the gloves. You put three sweets in a paper bag, and you hear yourself say, warmly, "Lovely."

ending.title: The New Host
ending.epitaph: Your host this evening, and every evening after.

end_every_day_november.title: Every Day Is November
end_every_day_november.text:
Between two strokes you slip out. Midnight does not let you go; it only fails to hold you. As the door closes Mr. Marrow says, kindly, "It comes due, you know."{{#if ribbon}} Dee's ribbon stays in your pocket, a promise with nowhere left to go.{{/if}}

Outside it is the first of November: cold sun, white sky, jack-o'-lanterns going soft on every step. You go home and go to bed. You wake, and it is the first of November, with the same pumpkins going soft and the same dog barking at the same bus.{{#if mirror}} No shop window shows you.{{/if}} Everyone else grows older around you, politely, while you stay in one bright cold day that never turns into the second.

ending.title: Every Day Is November
ending.epitaph: Got out on a technicality. Stayed out.

end_open_house.title: Open House
end_open_house.text:
You find the ring of the hatch under the cloth, and pull. You asked it up three times, and it is only accepting.

It comes up slowly, the way a guest comes up a garden path, unsure of its welcome and very glad of it, and it follows you home. It is very polite about it. It walks a little behind you, wearing your coat, and wipes its feet on your mat, and whoever opens your door says, without knowing why, "Well, come in, then." After that your house is warm. There is always something in the oven. The neighbours drop round, and stay, and stay. Everything smells, faintly and always, of warm bread and cloves.

ending.title: Open House
ending.epitaph: Something followed them home. It brought a casserole.

end_seat_at_table.title: Seat at the Table
end_seat_at_table.text:
You pick up your fork. It is the best thing you have ever tasted, and by the third mouthful you have stopped comparing it to anything, because there is nothing left to compare it with. There was a street once, and a voice calling you in. {{#if ribbon}}Somewhere a girl is still waiting on your promise. {{/if}}It goes the way breath goes off a window.

Mr. Marrow lays a gloved hand on the back of your chair. "Lovely," he says, and for once it means only that. Someone down the table passes you the bread. Your card is propped against your glass, and whatever it says is name enough. You are very happy. You are part of the furniture now.

end_paid_in_full.title: Paid in Full

ending.title: Paid in Full
ending.epitaph: Settled with what was owed: everything.

end_strangers_wages.title: Stranger's Wages
end_strangers_wages.text:
You shove the chair back and run before the napkin has settled, down the long table and out through the green door, and nobody stops you, because nobody has to.{{#if candle}} On the threshold the candle slips out of your fingers, and goes out.{{/if}}

The cellar beyond has never had a light in it. You find the shelves by touch, and the roots, which are warm, and you cannot find the stair. Far behind you a boy's voice says, without any malice at all, "One to the house."{{#if stance=treat}} "Our guest was playing after all," it adds, mildly.{{else}}{{#if lies>=2}} He counted every lie you told tonight, and enjoyed each one.{{else}}{{#if lied}} He counted your lie, too, and enjoyed it.{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}} The roots close round you, kindly, the way an armchair does.

ending.title: Stranger's Wages
ending.epitaph: Played the house. The house played back.
